METHODS: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) method was used to identify and select existing studies. Screening, data extraction, and synthesis were performed by three reviewers. Inclusion criteria covered original quantitative studies investigating social robots for depression in older adults. FINDINGS: Seven studies were identified-six randomized controlled trials and one comparison study-with all classified as good quality. CONCLUSIONS: The results highlight the potential of social robot interventions for reducing depression in older adults. However, the evidence is not strong enough to formulate recommendations on clinical effectiveness. text:
I read abstracts only, not full texts, so sample sizes and findings come from the abstracts. I kept studies where a social robot was used with people with a dementia diagnosis, or where the sample is described as dementia or mixed dementia/MCI. I dropped studies of older adults generally, such as the Hobbit home trials, the Zora evaluation, Brian 2.1, the Taiwanese Paro depression study, and the AIBO loneliness study. I also dropped studies that only gathered attitudes or design input.

## Overview

- **Paro dominates.** About two-thirds of the dementia studies I found use Paro, the robotic seal. The rest use robot pets (AIBO, a robot cat, Joy for All animals) or humanoid, conversational and companion robots (NAO, Ryan, MARIO, Matilda).
- **Most work is in care homes.** Day care and home settings are rare.
- **Results are mixed, and the designs are small.** Engagement, affect and social interaction improve fairly consistently. Symptom, physiological and quality-of-life outcomes are inconsistent.

## 1. Paro (robotic seal)

### Randomised or controlled designs

| Study | Setting and participants | Design | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jøranson et al. [W3088196398] (thesis: [W3102212853]) | 10 Norwegian nursing-home special care units; 60 residents with dementia | Cluster RCT; 30-min group sessions twice weekly for 12 weeks vs usual care | Better sleep on actigraphy: higher sleep efficiency and total sleep time, fewer night awakenings. The thesis also targets agitation, depression, psychotropic use and quality of life, but the abstract I retrieved gives no results for those. |
| Pu et al. [W3097289914] | 3 Australian nursing homes; 43 residents with dementia and chronic pain | Pilot RCT; individual 30-min sessions, 5 days/week for 6 weeks | Lower observed pain (PAINAD) and fewer as-needed medications. Staff-rated pain and scheduled medications did not differ. |
| Liang et al. [W2732925385] (thesis: [W2995685337]) | Dementia day care centres and homes in Auckland; 30 care-recipient/caregiver dyads | Pilot RCT, 12 weeks (Paro at day care and at home for 6 weeks) | Better facial affect and communication with staff at day care. No differences in dementia symptoms or physiological measures. People with less cognitive impairment responded better. The thesis reports little effect on caregiver well-being. |
| Moyle et al. [W1488883230] | Australian aged-care facility; 18 residents with moderate to severe dementia | Randomised crossover, Paro vs reading group | Moderate to large positive effect on quality of life and higher pleasure scores. |
| Valentí et al. [W1807810766] | Spanish nursing homes (101 and 110 patients) and day care (20 and 17 patients) | Non-randomised parallel arms: control, Paro, NAO, dog; 2 sessions/week for 3 months | Apathy improved in both robot groups. NAO group MMSE scores declined (sMMSE did not). In the day centre, NAO phase improved irritability and total NPI, and the Paro phase showed no differences. |
| Koh & Kang [W2894885829] | Korean nursing home; 33 residents with dementia | Non-equivalent control group; 12 sessions over 6 weeks | More positive emotion and social interaction, and fewer problem behaviours. |
| Takayanagi et al. [W1505024467] | Japanese care facility; 30 residents with mild/moderate or severe dementia | Paro vs stuffed lion, one-off interaction in the resident's room | Both groups talked more, laughed more and showed more positive emotion with Paro. The effect was visible in severe dementia too. |
| Thodberg et al. [W2294211165] | Danish nursing homes; 100 residents (dementia diagnoses recorded as a covariate) | RCT of visits with a dog, Paro or a toy cat; 12 visits | The dog and Paro drew the most touch, eye contact and talk. Paro lost residents' attention over time. More cognitive impairment meant more interaction with the animal and less with people. This is a mixed population, not dementia-only. |

### Observational, feasibility and qualitative studies

- **Šabanović et al. [W2040979576, W4243437205]:** Seven to eight weekly group sensory-therapy sessions in a US nursing home with 10 residents with varying dementia. Visual, verbal and physical interaction rose steadily, which argues against a pure novelty effect. Individuals used Paro in very different ways.
- **Yu et al. [W2080233792]:** A single session with community-dwelling people with MCI or mild-to-moderate dementia (n=11). Most stayed focused on Paro for the whole session and talked to it as a pet. Mood improved but not significantly.
- **Moyle et al. [W2778691880]:** Qualitative reflection on five participants from a cluster RCT (Paro vs plush toy vs usual care). Responses varied widely, and the same person could respond differently on different days. It also raises ethical questions about giving and retrieving Paro. I did not retrieve the trial's main quantitative report.
- **Pu et al. [W2985514812]:** Interviews with 11 residents from the pain trial above. They reported mood improvement and relaxation, and criticised Paro's weight and voice.

## 2. Other robot pets

- **AIBO:** Kramer et al. [W1972564462] compared a visitor alone, with a live dog, and with AIBO among female residents with dementia. Both animals stimulated more social interaction than the visitor alone. AIBO drew longer looks and more resident-initiated conversation than the dog. Naganuma et al. [W1178530349] used a remote-controlled AIBO in a dementia nursing home as a shared focus of attention that prompted communication between residents. That abstract gives no quantitative results.
- **Robotic cat (Libin & Cohen-Mansfield) [W2074069593]:** Pilot in a nursing home special care unit comparing a robotic cat with a plush cat. Both were linked to less agitation and more pleasure and interest, so the robot's added value is unclear.
- **Joy for All animals (Bradwell et al.) [W3015009700]:** Six months of diaries from two supported-living sites for people with dementia or learning difficulties. Use grew over time, with no sign of a novelty drop-off. Staff reported reminiscence, better communication and possibly less agitation or anxiety. Some people found the robots "creepy."
- **Robot cat at home (Pike et al.) [W3034490183]:** Qualitative case study of people with dementia and their families in their own homes. Themes were distraction, communication, acceptance and rejection, and connection. Benefits appeared where the cat was accepted.

## 3. Humanoid, conversational and companion robots

- **NAO:** Part of Valentí et al. [W1807810766] above. No clear benefit over Paro, and a possible cognitive decline signal.
- **MARIO (Irish nursing home):** In the quantitative pilot [W2955051104], 10 residents had up to 12 sessions over 4 weeks (music, news, reminiscence, games, calendar). They stayed engaged and accepted the robot and spent more time socially engaged. Quality of life, depression and perceived social support did not change significantly. The qualitative evaluation [W2889731820] interviewed residents, relatives, carers and managers. Attitudes were largely positive, and the authors framed MARIO as having potential against loneliness.
- **Ryan Companionbot [W2771925981]:** Six people with moderate dementia and/or depression in a senior living facility had 24/7 access to the robot for 4–6 weeks. They built rapport and valued it. This is observational and interview data only.
- **Matilda [W2564685734]:** Trialled 2010–2013 with 115 participants in Australian residential aged care. Emotional, visual and behavioural engagement improved significantly over the years, and acceptance was high. The abstract frames the work around dementia but does not give a dementia-only sample.
- **Autonomous robot in a walking group (Hebesberger et al.) [W4251569456]:** Deployed for a month with two weekly walking groups of older adults with advanced dementia at a care site. Therapists saw gains in motivation, group cohesion and mood. Unreliable robot performance quickly added to staff workload.
- **Conversational robot for Alzheimer's (Pou-Prom et al.) [W3033476063]:** Pilot of a cognitive-assessment conversation. Human partners produced better conversations, but participants liked the robot and stayed interested despite miscommunication.

## 4. Reviews that include dementia

- **Alonso et al. [W2888482633]:** Systematic review of social robots for ageing and dementia. It reports mostly positive findings on acceptance, independence and stress.
- **Abdi et al. [W2789445850]:** Scoping review of 33 studies, 11 robots and 1,574 participants. 28 of the 33 studies reported positive findings, with many methodological problems. It identified five roles: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy.
- **Pu et al. [W2808281222]:** Meta-analysis of RCTs in older adults generally. It found no statistically significant pooled effects on agitation, anxiety or quality of life, and the evidence was low quality.

## 5. Borderline or excluded

- **Protocol only:** [W2975531399] is a protocol for a humanoid robot vs tablet training for people with dementia at home. It reports no results.
- **Dementia status unclear:** Tapus & Matarić's robot music therapist [W759765632] is described as being for cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's, but the abstract is too brief to judge. The Paro nursing-home field studies [W2039822570, W2043587319] and Brian 2.1's memory game [W2003566851] involve long-term care residents, but their abstracts do not say they have dementia. Kuwahara's communication robots [W2585556435] have no results.
- **Staff views only:** Jung et al. [W2689483015] surveyed and interviewed clinicians about Paro.

## Gaps and cautions

- **Evidence base:** It is small and mostly pilot-scale. Only the Norwegian sleep trial and the Australian pain trial are larger RCTs.
- **Comparators:** Several studies use a plush toy or other animal comparator, and the results suggest the robot's advantage over a soft toy is not always clear.
- **Individual differences:** Cognitive level, preferences and staff mediation shape the response. This theme runs through [W2732925385, W2778691880, W2294211165, W2985514812].
- **Under-studied areas:** Home use, caregiver outcomes, long-term follow-up, and non-pet robots all have few studies.
- **Possible missing trials:** I did not retrieve some well-known Paro and robot-pet trials. A targeted search for particular authors or trials would help.

As I said above, there was no first map. The list below is what I retrieved but left out of the dementia-only write-up. While checking it, I found that I had skipped several dementia-relevant papers by oversight. The oversight was mine. Those papers did meet your criteria.

## A. Dementia papers I missed, now checked and added

- **Inoue et al. [W4407738599]:** Occupational therapy with patients with dementia, comparing Paro with a stuffed animal. The authors conclude that robot therapy differs from therapy with inanimate objects and can make patients more self-directive. The abstract gives no sample size or measures.
- **Tummers-Heemels et al. [W3198896322]:** Two qualitative studies. One compares responses of people with dementia to a live dog and a robotic companion in a care home. The other is a longitudinal case study of one person with Alzheimer's bonding with a robot pet. The authors report enrichment of social and emotional life, from very small samples.
- **Khosla et al. [W1994379356]:** Matilda deployed in several Australian households for six months to support people with dementia at home. The authors report sensory enrichment, social connection and respite for partners. This adds to the residential Matilda study I already included [W2564685734]. The abstract gives no numbers.
- **Broadbent et al. symposium [W2791822482]:** A conference abstract summarising four projects. It includes a pre-post study of a companion robot on loneliness and quality of life, and cognitive-stimulation robots tested in real settings. It is too thin to treat as a study.

## B. Dropped as unclear or not usable

- **Lee & Davis, "Sunshine" chat robot [W3041860695]:** A pilot with older adults with cognitive impairment in long-term care. The retrieved text is only the opening of a letter, so I cannot tell whether it meets your criteria. Check the full text.
- **Prescott et al., MiRo [W2895915058]:** A development abstract about a dementia-oriented robot, with no study with people with dementia.
- **Casey et al., MARIO focus groups [W2484033910]:** Design focus groups with people with dementia, with no robot use.
- **Mion et al. [W2900350517]:** A lab test of a robot, with 8% of participants having dementia.
- **Also dropped for being design, development or protocol papers:** [W2931420217, W2094053894, W2760294871, W2975531399, W2172131195].

## C. Dropped because the population was older adults generally

These involve actual robot use, but not people with dementia.

- **Home and independent living:** Hobbit trials [W2994761079, W3137166629]; the companion robot field test with 8 seniors [W2717439789]; the Paro in-home study with depressed older adults [W2953482672]; the robot-delivered cognitive test [W2924547041]; the medication-adherence robot trial [W1558982838].

This covers [W2521240520, W1575107006, W2068857685, W2049072188, W2734517545, W3093570108, W2893222310, W2976777638] and similar papers. Some involve people with dementia or MCI, but as respondents rather than robot users. W2521240520, W2068857685 and the MARIO focus groups [W2484033910] are the closest to your interest if you later want an acceptance strand.

You're right, the first turn ended without a written answer. I'm sorry about that. Below is the overview for older people in general. As before, I read abstracts only. The dementia-specific studies are in my previous report, so here I only point to them.

## Scope and scale

The broader literature is large, and I did not retrieve all of it. The two best overviews I found are:

- **Abdi et al. scoping review [W2789445850]:** 33 studies, 11 robots and 1,574 participants. 28 of the 33 reported positive findings, but many had methodological problems. It identified five roles for social robots: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy.
- **Pu et al. meta-analysis [W2808281222]:** 11 RCTs. Pooled effects on agitation, anxiety and quality of life were not significant. Narrative synthesis suggested better engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and less loneliness and medication use. Bias risk was high.

I organise the studies below by what the robot was used for.

## 1. Robot pets and companions in care settings

| Study | Robot | Participants and setting | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wada & Shibata [W2043711811] | Two seal robots (Paro) | Residents of a Japanese care house; robots active over 9 h/day; first-month results | Social interaction increased. Urinary stress-hormone tests improved. |
| Sung et al. [W1510372641] | Paro | 16 institutionalised older adults (12 completed); group sessions twice weekly for 4 weeks; one-group pre-post | Communication/interaction skills and activity participation improved. |
| Chen et al. [W3015603533] | Paro, kept by each participant 24/7 | 20 older adults with depression in 4 Taiwanese long-term care facilities; 8 weeks observation then 8 weeks intervention | Depression and loneliness fell and quality of life rose during the intervention period, but not during the observation period. Interviews reported companionship and more social interaction. |
| Randall et al. [W2953482672] | Paro plus sensors | 10 older adults with clinical depression, in their own homes for one month | People without pets used Paro more and had more positive attitudes. Companionship alone was not enough to sustain long-term use for many. |
| Banks et al. [W2132164645] | AIBO vs live dog vs control | Long-term care residents | Loneliness fell in both the dog and AIBO groups versus controls. Attachment did not explain the change. |
| Broadbent et al. [W1945345301] | Six different health-care robots (entertainment, communication, monitoring) | 53 residents and 53 staff, one aged-care facility; non-randomised, 12 weeks | No significant benefits or harms. Staff job satisfaction rose only in the control group. Responses to the robots were mixed. |
| Huisman & Kort [W2915888239] | Zora (a NAO with software) | 14 Dutch nursing care organisations, two years; interviews, questionnaires and observation | Barriers included start-up time and software failures. Staff reported a positive effect on clients and that using it made work more fun. |
| Ostrowski et al. [W2943699887] | A social robot (the abstract does not name it) | Assisted-living community, long-term | The study asks whether the robot can foster human-to-human connection. The abstract gives no results. |

## 2. Humanoid robots for social, cognitive and mood activities

- **Fields et al. [W2982896790]:** NAO ran a three-session Shakespeare activity with 15 residents aged 65+. Mood scores improved significantly across sessions and depression scores fell marginally. People with and without dementia took part, so this is a mixed sample.
- **Louie, McColl & Nejat [W2003566851, W2112421347]:** The expressive human-like robot Brian 2.1 in a long-term care facility. In the mealtime study, 8 residents aged 82–93 were engaged, complied with the robot and enjoyed it. The memory-game case study focused on acceptability of the robot as a cognitive training tool, and the abstract gives no results.
- **van Maris et al. [W3001702224]:** Two retirement villages, 8 sessions over 4 weeks, comparing emotive and non-emotive robot behaviour. Behaviour did not affect acceptance or attachment. Attachment stayed low to medium, and perceived ease of use rose over time.

## 3. Exercise and physical activity coaches

- **Fasola & Matarić [W2065178260, W2033159471]:** A robot coach for seated arm exercise, tested with elderly participants. Users strongly preferred a relational coach, with praise and personal discourse, over a non-relational one. They gave high ratings for enjoyment and companionship.
- **Gadde et al. [W2025048472]:** A proof-of-concept exercise-demonstration robot with 10 participants. Usability testing supported feasibility, and a controlled trial was only planned.
- **Avioz-Sarig et al. [W3089483243]:** NAO and Poppy as exercise coaches with 32 older adults. Both motivated engagement, and the type and timing of feedback mattered. Most preferred the more mechanical-looking Poppy.
- **Olde Keizer et al. [W2939831007]:** NAO versus a tablet for health monitoring and training tasks with 20 frail older adults. Usability was average for both, and enjoyment was high. NAO's speech interaction caused most problems, such as its limited vocabulary and difficulty with Dutch dialect. Seven people preferred NAO.
- **Piezzo & Suzuki [W2731113721]:** Pepper as a walking guide in a first feasibility study. It reports user feedback and basic gait analysis, but the abstract gives no results.
- **Bhattacharjee Chen et al. [W2766970278]:** 16 healthy older adults led a mobile manipulator in a partner-dance stepping task. They found it useful, easy to use and enjoyable.

## 4. Home service and independent-living robots

| Study | Robot | Participants and setting | Findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bajones et al. [W2994761079]; Pripfl et al. [W3137166629] | Hobbit (autonomous mobile, with manipulation) | 16 households (multi-week) and 18 households (371 days in total), age 75+ | All users interacted with Hobbit daily and rated most functions as working well. In the earlier trial it was seen more as a toy than as support for independent living. Perceived safety did not rise, and the prototype was slow and not robust. Users believed a market-ready version would help more fragile people. |
| Zsiga et al. [W2717439789] | Companion robot with voice interaction | 8 seniors living alone, about 95 days each | Accepted enthusiastically. Entertainment, locomotion and weather forecast were used most. Navigation and speech recognition were the least reliable and need improvement. |
| Beer et al. [W2757061426] | Mobile manipulator (demonstration only) | Older adults, pre/post exposure | Acceptance rose after seeing the robot perform tasks. |
| Cavallo et al. [W2811507747] | Robot-Era robots (domestic, condominium and outdoor) | 35 older users, six services, three environments | Appearance and acceptance scores were positive, and services averaged above 80/100. Scores varied by education and sex. |
| Jayawardena et al. [W1982844896] | HealthBot v2 | Retirement-village field trials | The abstract reports promising acceptance but no figures. |
| Broadbent et al. [W1558982838] | Robots in older people's homes | Randomised crossover trial of medication adherence and quality of life | No abstract was available, so I cannot report findings. |

## 5. Telepresence and monitoring

- **Cortellessa et al. [W2743226003]:** ROBIN, a telepresence robot built on Giraff, was assessed by 25 users. It was judged usable and pleasant, with limited workload, and open-minded users interacted more positively.
- **Cesta et al. [W2259814160]:** A one-year Giraff case study used to validate an evaluation methodology. The abstract gives no outcome results.
- **Bäck et al. [W2322289952]:** A humanoid robot answered alarms in three Finnish nursing homes (29 alarms in total). It navigated correctly, opened the voice connection and sent images. Residents' responses were uniformly positive.

## 6. Robot-led assessment and data collection

- **Boumans et al. [W2946005838]:** A social robot collected patient-reported outcomes from 31 community-dwelling people aged 70+, in a crossover against human-administered questionnaires. Data reliability was 99.6% and usability averaged 80.1/100.
- **Takaeda et al. [W2924547041]:** A robot administered a speech-based cognitive test (Japanese TICS) to older adults from retirement homes and adult day care. 66 took part in experiment 1 and 40 in experiment 2. Reliability was satisfactory (test-retest 0.818), and over half wanted the robot version. The researcher still timed the questions and scored answers.

## Cross-cutting patterns

- **Robot types:** Paro dominates the affective and companion work, followed by AIBO. Humanoids (NAO, Pepper, Brian, Poppy, Zora) dominate coaching and cognitive activities. Mobile service robots (Hobbit, Robot-Era) dominate home studies.
- **Settings:** Care homes and long-term care are the commonest. Home studies are fewer and are mostly feasibility or acceptance studies.
- **Outcomes:** Engagement, acceptance and social interaction are the most consistent positives. Clinical outcomes such as depression, loneliness and quality of life improve in some small uncontrolled studies and not in others [W1945345301].
- **Practical findings:** Reliability, speed and speech recognition are repeated barriers [W2994761079, W3137166629, W2717439789, W2915888239, W2939831007].
- **Study quality:** Samples are mostly under 40 and many designs are one-group or short. The reviews [W2789445850, W2808281222] say the same.

## Caveats

- Several papers I classed as older-adult studies use samples that include people with cognitive impairment or dementia. Fields et al. [W2982896790] says so explicitly. The care-home studies often do not report it.
- I left out studies of attitudes only, ethics and design, and development papers with no user study. I can add them if you want an acceptance strand.
- I did not cover some topics, such as telepresence beyond Giraff, humanoids in hospital settings, or trials since 2020. A targeted search could fill these.

I can merge this with the dementia report into a single table, or look for more RCTs outside the Paro literature.
